title: Discovery of the Atom
lead: Atoms were proposed by the ancient Greeks more than two thousand years before anyone could detect one. The evidence for them grew from the fixed mass ratios of chemistry, the periodic table and kinetic theory to the jiggling of pollen grains in water.
objectives: Describe the basic structure of the atom, the substructure of all matter.
summary_html:
• Atoms are the smallest unit of elements; atoms combine to form molecules, the smallest unit of compounds.
  • The first direct observation of atoms was in Brownian motion.
  • Analysis of Brownian motion gave accurate sizes for atoms ($10^{-10}\;\text{m}$ on average) and a precise value for Avogadro’s number.

figures.original_caption: The position of a pollen grain in water, measured every few seconds under a microscope, exhibits Brownian motion. Brownian motion is due to fluctuations in the number of atoms and molecules colliding with a small mass, causing it to move about in complex paths. This is nearly direct evidence for the existence of atoms, providing a satisfactory alternative explanation cannot be found.

exercises.prompt: Name three different types of evidence for the existence of atoms.

answer.solution: The fixed mass ratios of reactants in chemical reactions point to basic units that combine in those ratios. The periodic table, whose patterns predicted elements before they were found, and kinetic theory, which explains the gas laws and thermodynamics from atoms and molecules in random thermal motion, are further indirect evidence. Brownian motion, the jiggling of a small particle struck unevenly by the molecules around it, is direct evidence, as are mass spectrometers that detect individual ions and microscopes that image individual atoms.

exercises.prompt: Explain why patterns observed in the periodic table of the elements are evidence for the existence of atoms, and why Brownian motion is a more direct type of evidence for their existence.

answer.solution: The periodic table shows that the properties of elements repeat in a regular way, and it predicted elements that were later found with the predicted properties. Such order is what we would expect if each element were made of one kind of basic unit with a definite structure, but it only infers atoms from the behavior of large amounts of matter. In Brownian motion we watch a single visible particle being pushed about, first this way, then that, by uneven numbers of molecules striking its sides. We still do not see the molecules, but we see the effect of their individual collisions, and the motion can be analyzed to give their size, so it is much closer to observing them directly.

exercises.prompt: If atoms exist, why can’t we see them with visible light?

answer.solution: An atom is about $10^{-10}$ m across, while the wavelengths of visible light run from about 380 to 760 nm, several thousand times larger. A wave cannot resolve details much smaller than its wavelength, since it diffracts around them, so no microscope using visible light can show an individual atom, however good its lenses.
